solutions.question: 1(a)
solutions.latex: The graph of $y=\sqrt{4-x}$ exists only for $x\le 4$ and has its endpoint at $(4,0)$, so the answer is B.

solutions.question: 1(b)
solutions.latex:
$$A=\int_0^2 (4-2x)\,dx+\int_2^6 (2x-4)\,dx=\left[4x-x^2\right]_0^2+\left[x^2-4x\right]_2^6=4+12-(-4)=20\ \text{units}^2$$

Alternatively, from the graph the area is two triangles: $A=\tfrac12\times 2\times 4+\tfrac12\times 4\times 8=20\ u^2$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: correct area 20; 1: correct set-up (integrals or triangle areas)

solutions.question: 1(d)
solutions.latex:
$$\int_{-1}^{2} f(x)\,dx=\int_{-1}^{0} f(x)\,dx+\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx+\int_1^2 f(x)\,dx=2\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx+\int_1^2 f(x)\,dx$$

$$=2\times\tfrac12+\left(-\tfrac32\right)=-\tfrac12$$

solutions.question: 1(e)
solutions.latex:
Translating $b$ units left: $8(x+b)^2$; dilating horizontally by factor $a$: $8\left(\dfrac{x}{a}+b\right)^2$; translating $c$ units up: $8\left(\dfrac{x}{a}+b\right)^2+c$.

$$8\left(\dfrac{x}{a}+b\right)^2+c\equiv 2x^2+4x+21 \iff \dfrac{8}{a^2}x^2+\dfrac{16b}{a}x+(8b^2+c)\equiv 2x^2+4x+21$$

$\dfrac{8}{a^2}=2\Rightarrow a=2$ (since $a>0$); $\dfrac{16b}{a}=4\Rightarrow b=\tfrac12$; $8b^2+c=21\Rightarrow c=19$.

So $a=2$, $b=\tfrac12$, $c=19$. (The alternative working with a translation $b$ to the right gives $a=2$, $b=-\tfrac12$, $c=19$.)

solutions.question: 2(c)

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=6x^2-12x=0$, i.e. $6x(x-2)=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=2$. Also $y(0)=0$ and $y(2)=-8$, so $(0,0)$ and $(2,-8)$ are the stationary points.

$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12x-12$, which is $-12<0$ when $x=0$ and $12>0$ when $x=2$.

By the second derivative test, $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point and $(2,-8)$ is a minimum turning point. (A table of values of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ either side of each point is an equivalent justification.)
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: stationary points found (1); second derivative (1); nature of both points (1)

solutions.latex: A necessary condition is $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$, so $12x-12=0$, i.e. $x=1$. Also $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$ when $x>1$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}<0$ when $x<1$, so the concavity changes at $x=1$. Hence $(1,-4)$ is a point of inflection. (Equivalently, evaluate the second derivative either side of $x=1$.)
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: point of inflection (1); justification by change in concavity (1)

solutions.question: 4(a)
solutions.latex: Solving $x^2-2x=-x^2+4$ gives $2x^2-2x-4=0$, so $2(x-2)(x+1)=0$, hence $x=-1$ or $x=2$, as required. (Equivalently, substitute $x=-1$ and $x=2$ into both equations to show common $y$-coordinates.)

solutions.question: 5(b)
solutions.latex:
$P$ is minimised when $\dfrac{dP}{dx}=0$.

$$\dfrac{dP}{dx}=-4000+5000\times\tfrac12(36+x^2)^{-1/2}\times 2x=\dfrac{5000x}{\sqrt{36+x^2}}-4000=0$$

$\dfrac{5x}{\sqrt{36+x^2}}=4\iff 25x^2=16(36+x^2)\iff 9x^2=576\iff x^2=64\iff x=\pm8$. Since $x\in[0,10]$, $x=8$ only.

Justification of minimum (first derivative test): at $x=7$, $\dfrac{dP}{dx}\approx-204<0$; at $x=9$, $\dfrac{dP}{dx}\approx160>0$. So a relative minimum occurs at $x=8$, i.e. $CD=8$ km.

Optional: $P(0)=\$70\,000$, $P(10)\approx\$58\,310$, $P(8)=\$58\,000$, so $x=8$ gives the absolute minimum on $[0,10]$. (Second derivative test: $\dfrac{d^2P}{dx^2}=\dfrac{180\,000}{(36+x^2)^{3/2}}$, which equals $180>0$ at $x=8$.)
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: derivative set to zero (1); solving to $x=8$ (1); justification of minimum (1)
